title: Heaps and Top-k Selection: Visual Guide
outline: Title: Heaps and Top-k Selection: Visual Guide

1. How Much Order | six operations run against a hash map, a sorted array and a binary heap on n = 1,000,000, with cost bars on a log scale | the heap is the middle of the order/cost trade — O(1) peek and O(log n) update, O(n) search — so a promise you never make is a promise you never pay for

2. Sift Up, Sift Down | a seven-step trace inserting 3 into [2,5,4,12,9,7] and then extracting the minimum, with the tree, the array, the index arithmetic and a tap-any-cell parent/child calculator | insert appends then sifts up and extract-min promotes the last element then sifts down against the SMALLER child, each touching one root-to-leaf path in O(log n)

3. The Admission Threshold | a bounded min-heap with a k slider stepping the stream 8, 2, 5, 10, 7, 1, showing admit/discard verdicts, the root as cutoff, and running comparison and replacement counts | capping a MIN-heap at k makes the root the weakest current winner, giving O(1) rejection for most candidates, O(n log k) time and O(k) memory in one online pass

4. Heap Versus Full Sort | sliders over n and k plotting n log2 n against n log2 k in comparison units, with retained-memory pills and the k = n meeting point | the heap's advantage is proportional to how much smaller k is than n, it vanishes at k = n where full sorting is the honest operation, and the winners still come out heap-ordered rather than ranked

5. Choosing The Algorithm | three real scenarios — a 10M streamed iterator needing 100, an export of every record in order, and one resident 1M batch needing 1,000 — scored across full sort, quickselect and a bounded heap | the decisive questions are how much order the consumer needs and how the data arrives, which is why quickselect wins on a resident batch and only the heap works on a stream
